tests.name: test_filled
tests.description: choices gives a list, not None.

tests.name: test_pairs
tests.description: choices(["a", "b", "c", "d"], 2) gives the 6 pairs in this order: ["a", "b"], ["a", "c"], ["a", "d"], ["b", "c"], ["b", "d"] and ["c", "d"].
tests.message: choices(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'], 2) gives [], not the 6 pairs from ['a', 'b'] to ['c', 'd'].

tests.name: test_ends
tests.description: Choosing 0 items gives one set, the empty one; choosing all of them gives one set, all of them; and choosing more items than there are gives no sets.

tests.name: test_counts
tests.description: A list of n items has math.comb(n, k) sets of k items, for every n up to 10 and every k from 0 to n + 1.

tests.name: test_library
tests.description: choices(items, k) agrees with Python's itertools.combinations(items, k), set for set and in the same order, for lists of up to 8 items and every k.

tests.name: test_all_subsets
tests.description: A list of 10 items has 1,024 sets of every size together, 2 to the power 10, and none comes twice.
tests.message: choices gives 0 sets of the 10 items across every k from 0 to 10, not 1,024.

tests.name: test_unchanged
tests.description: choices leaves the list it is given as it was.

tests.name: test_five_two
tests.description: choose(5, 2) is 10, as the Explore phase counted.

tests.name: test_whole
tests.description: choose gives an int, a whole number, not a float.
tests.message: choose(10, 3) gives 120.0, a float, not an int. The / operator always gives a float, while // keeps whole numbers whole.

tests.name: test_triangle
tests.description: choose(n, k) is right for every n from 0 to 12 and every k from 0 to n, checked against Pascal's triangle.

tests.name: test_too_many
tests.description: choose(n, k) is 0 when k is more than n, since there is no way to choose more things than there are.

tests.name: test_library
tests.description: choose(n, k) agrees with Python's math.comb(n, k) for every n up to 60 and every k from 0 to n.

tests.name: test_short_way
tests.description: choose(n, k) with n = 1,000,000 and k = 999,998 is 499,999,500,000, found by choosing the 2 left out, in 2 passes of the loop rather than 999,998.

tests.name: test_own_work
tests.description: choose works the count out itself, without Python's own counting functions: math.comb, math.perm (which counts ordered choices) or math.factorial.

tests.name: test_next
tests.description: next_row gives the row below: [1] gives [1, 1], [1, 1] gives [1, 2, 1], and [1, 3, 3, 1] gives [1, 4, 6, 4, 1].

tests.name: test_unchanged
tests.description: next_row leaves the row it is given as it was.
tests.message: After next_row(row) with row = [1, 3, 3, 1], row has become [1, 4, 6, 4, 1]. Build the new row as a new list, and only read from row.

tests.name: test_rows
tests.description: triangle(n) gives rows 0 to n, which is n + 1 rows, and row i has i + 1 entries.
tests.message: Row 0 of triangle(1) is [1, 1], not a list of 1 entry.

tests.name: test_counts
tests.description: Row n, place k of triangle(30) is math.comb(n, k), for every n up to 30 and every k from 0 to n.
tests.message: Row 0 of triangle(30) has 31 entries, not 1.

tests.name: test_sums
tests.description: Row n of triangle(20) adds up to 2 to the power n, for every n up to 20.
tests.message: Row 0 of triangle(20) adds up to 1,048,576, not 1.

tests.name: test_separate
tests.description: The rows of triangle(5) are separate lists, so changing one leaves the others as they were.
tests.message: triangle(5) gives [[1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1], [1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1], [1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1], [1, 5, 10, 1…, not rows 0 to 5, so this test cannot change row 2 yet.

tests.name: test_pairs
tests.description: arrangements(["a", "b", "c"], 2) gives the 6 ordered pairs: ["a", "b"], ["a", "c"], ["b", "a"], ["b", "c"], ["c", "a"] and ["c", "b"].
tests.message: arrangements(['a', 'b', 'c'], 2) gives [['a', 'b'], ['a', 'c'], ['b', 'c']], not the 6 ordered pairs.

tests.name: test_podiums
tests.description: There are 720 podiums of 3 from 10 models, 10 × 9 × 8, each with 3 different models, and none comes twice.
tests.message: arrangements of 3 from 10 items gives 120 choices, not 720.

tests.name: test_orders
tests.description: 4 items have 4! = 24 orders, and arrangements(items, 4) gives every one of them.

tests.name: test_too_many
tests.description: There is no way to choose more items than there are, so arrangements(items, k) is [] when k is more than the number of items.

tests.name: test_library
tests.description: arrangements(items, k) agrees with Python's itertools.permutations(items, k), choice for choice and in the same order, for lists of up to 6 items and every k from 0 to 7.
